transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, honestly, I... I didn't even think I needed to make this appointment, but it's this whole insurance situation. I had to get a routine physical done for my health insurance—you know how they make you jump through all those hoops now, checking every little thing before they'll finalize your coverage. Anyway, I went in to see the doctor they sent me to, and he gets me on the scale and starts telling me that my weight is too low. 

Which, I mean, I just don't see it at all. I'm a painter, right? Residential and commercial. So I'm up and down ladders all day long, carrying heavy five-gallon buckets of primer, stretching, reaching... it's a very physical line of work. And the days are incredibly long, especially right now when we're trying to finish exterior jobs before the sun goes down. Sometimes I'm out on a site for ten or twelve hours straight. So, yeah, of course I'm going to be lean. To me, I just look like a guy who works hard for a living, you know? I've always been on the move, even back when I was taking some college classes years ago, but now it's just pure physical labor every single day. 

But this insurance doctor, he just got completely hung up on the number on the scale and insisted I come talk to someone about it. So... here I am, just trying to get the paperwork cleared up, really.
Do you think your weight is normal for you?

Normal? I mean, yeah, I really do think it's normal for me. At least, normal for the kind of life I'm living right now. I know that insurance doctor was all worked up about it, and, honestly, it's not just him. Some of my buddies from the crew—and even a couple of friends I've known since my college days—have been making these little comments lately. Like, "Hey man, you're looking a little thin," or "Are you taking breaks to eat out there?" They get all worried, texting me, asking if I'm okay. 

But I just feel like everyone is completely overreacting. I really do. It's like they see a number on a chart or they notice my face looks a little leaner, and suddenly it's panic mode. But if there was actually a problem, wouldn't I be too weak to work? Because I am out there every single day. I'm showing up to my jobs at 6 AM, I'm unloading the truck, I'm hauling those massive extension ladders by myself—which, by the way, are not light, especially the heavy-duty aluminum ones we have to use for those older three-story Victorians downtown. 

I'm getting all my work done, I'm keeping the crew on schedule, and I'm not missing a beat. So how could my weight be this huge medical crisis if I'm still functioning perfectly fine? I just think if my body was really in danger, I wouldn't be able to put in a twelve-hour shift of pure manual labor, you know? It just doesn't make any logical sense to me why they're making such a massive deal out of it when my work performance hasn't slipped one bit. I'm still doing exactly what I need to do.
Do you ever look in the mirror and think you look too thin?

Too thin? No, no, definitely not. If anything, it's the exact opposite, honestly. I mean, I spend a lot of time looking in the mirror—probably more than I should, if I'm being totally real with you. It's just... well, my morning routine is pretty involved. I get up super early, way before the sun is even thinking about coming up, and while I'm getting ready, brushing my teeth, washing my face, I can't help but really scrutinize how I look. 

And it's not just the mirror in my bathroom, either. It's photos, too. Like, a lot of times when we finish a big commercial job or a really intricate residential exterior, I'll take pictures of myself standing next to the work. It's good for the portfolio, you know? Showing the scale of the building and the guy who actually did the work. But when I look at those pictures, or when I'm standing there in my bathroom at 5 AM under those harsh overhead lights, I am hyper-focused on my stomach and my face. 

I'm looking to see if everything looks... sharp. Tight, you know? Like, if my jawline isn't defined enough, or if my stomach looks even a little bit soft or bloated, it completely ruins my headspace for the entire day. I will literally judge how the rest of my day is going to go based on that one look in the mirror. If I look sharp and lean, I feel great, I feel energized, I'm ready to tackle a twelve-hour shift. But if I don't... man, it just hangs over me. I feel sluggish, I feel heavy, even if the scale hasn't changed. So, no, I never look at myself and think, "Oh, I'm too thin." I'm always looking to make sure I don't look soft. Because in my line of work, you can't be soft. You have to be solid.
Are you afraid of gaining weight?

Well, afraid is a strong word, but... I mean, I definitely don't want to gain weight. I keep a really close eye on it, actually. It's just part of being disciplined, I think. Like, sometimes, you know, we'll finish a really big job—maybe a whole commercial complex that took us three weeks of solid, backbreaking work—and the client will want to take the crew out to dinner to celebrate. Or maybe one of the guys brings in a bunch of bagels or something for the morning meeting. And, you know, I try to be polite, I don't want to make a big deal out of it, so I'll eat some of it. Maybe I'll have a little bread at the dinner, or half a bagel. 

But then, the next morning, when I do my whole routine and step on the scale... if that number has gone up, even just a tiny fraction of a pound, I can feel this tightness right in my chest. It just makes me so tense. My whole body just kind of locks up, and I start running through everything I ate the day before, calculating it all out in my head. And I immediately—I mean, right then and there, standing in the bathroom—I make a plan to cut back for the rest of the day, or even the next couple of days. I'll skip lunch, or I'll just have black coffee until dinner, whatever it takes. Because I just can't let that extra weight stick. If I let it stick once, then what's stopping it from happening again? And before you know it, you're soft, you're sluggish, you can't haul the ladders... so, yeah, I guess you could say I'm pretty motivated to make sure the scale never goes up. I just have to stay on top of it.
Does worrying about gaining weight ever interfere with your daily activities or relationships?

Interfere? I mean... I wouldn't say it interferes with my work, if that's what you mean. Like I said, I'm still getting all my painting jobs done. The prep work, the priming, the edging, the cleanup—I'm on top of all of it. I haven't missed a deadline, and my clients are always happy with the final product. So functionally, professionally, everything is completely fine. I'm still the guy they call when they need a big job done right and done fast.

But... I guess, on the social side of things, it does get a little complicated. Like, I was talking earlier about those client dinners, right? When we finish a big project, especially the commercial ones where the general contractor is feeling generous, they always want to take the crew out. Or even just my buddies wanting to grab a beer and some wings after a long Friday. Lately... well, I've just been avoiding them. I'll make up an excuse, say I've got another estimate to write up, or that I need to organize the van, or that I'm just beat and need to hit the sack early. 

And it's not that I don't want to hang out with the guys. I do. We've been through a lot of tough jobs together. But if I go to those dinners, or out for drinks, it just turns into a whole... thing. You know? Because I'm trying to be careful about what I eat, so I'll just order a salad with no dressing, or maybe just sip on a diet soda while everyone else is housing burgers and fries. And then the comments start. "Is that all you're eating?" "Come on, man, live a little!" "You're already so thin, you can afford a burger!" 

And then it just spirals into them scrutinizing how I look, and bringing up my weight again, and it's just exhausting. I don't want to sit there and defend my choices or have my body become the topic of conversation for an hour while I'm just trying to relax after a sixty-hour work week. So, yeah, I just avoid those situations entirely now. It's just easier to go home, stick to my routine, and not have to deal with the Spanish Inquisition over a plate of hot wings, you know? It's just about protecting my peace of mind, really.
Do you often restrict the amount of food you eat to avoid gaining weight?

Well, restrict... I mean, I guess it depends on how you look at it. I just look at it as being efficient, honestly. Because my days are long, and they start early. If I'm going to be on a ladder by 7 AM, taping off ceilings and cutting in around all the trim, I can't be weighed down. 

So, most days, I really just keep it to coffee in the morning. Just black coffee. It gets me going, keeps me sharp, and I don't have to worry about feeling heavy. And then, you know, the day just gets going. You're mixing, you're rolling, you're constantly moving up and down the scaffolding. If I get hungry between paint jobs, or maybe if I'm just sitting in the van waiting for a coat of primer to dry on some cabinets, I might have a protein bar. Just something quick I can unwrap and eat without really thinking about it. 

Because, to be completely honest with you, eating a full meal during the day just feels like it would totally slow me down. If I were to stop and eat a big lunch—like a heavy sub or whatever the other guys are getting from the deli—it just sits there in my gut. I can literally feel it every time I bend over to load my roller from the tray. It makes me feel sluggish, like I'm dragging extra weight around, and I start worrying that it's just going to stick to me and make me soft. I can't afford to lose my momentum like that. I need to stay light on my feet, especially when I'm hauling five-gallon buckets of latex paint up two flights of stairs. 

And then by the time I get home, I'll just have a really small dinner. Just a little something, nothing heavy. Because if I eat a big dinner, I know I'm going to wake up the next morning feeling bloated, and then I'll step on the scale, and the number might be up, and then my whole headspace is ruined for the next day, just like I was telling you earlier. So keeping it really tight—just the coffee, the bar, the small dinner—it just works better for me. It keeps the weight off and keeps me moving fast. People think painting is just slapping color on a wall, but it's incredibly physical, and you just can't do it right if you're weighed down by food. So, yeah, I guess I do limit what I eat, but it's really just what makes sense for how I need to operate.
Do you think about your weight or body shape every day?

Every day? Yeah... I mean, I don't think there's an hour that goes by where it's not somewhere in the back of my mind. It’s... well, you have to understand, my whole livelihood is completely visual. I spend my entire day looking at surfaces, checking for tiny imperfections, making sure the edges are perfectly straight and sharp. And I guess... I guess that way of seeing things just bleeds over into how I look at myself. 

Like, I do a lot of custom work, right? Sometimes these really big, intricate murals for local businesses—cafes, gyms, maybe a big feature wall in a corporate office. I took a few art and design classes back in college before I started painting houses full-time, so I get tapped for these specialty jobs pretty often. And whenever I finish one, the owners always want to take pictures for their social media or whatever. You know, "Here’s the guy with the finished wall!" And I’ll stand next to this mural that I just spent maybe eighty hours perfecting... but when they show me the photo on their phone? I’m not even looking at the artwork. I am zeroing right in on my body. 

If I see that photo, or even if I’m just cutting in around a big vanity mirror in a client’s master bathroom and I catch my reflection by accident... I immediately start analyzing my stomach and my face. I just need to see if I look sharp. If my jawline isn't totally defined, or if my stomach doesn't look perfectly flat, it honestly just dictates my entire mood. I will literally judge the whole day by whether my stomach and face look sharp enough in that moment. It doesn't matter if the client just handed me a massive tip or if I painted the best mural of my life. If I look even a little bit soft in that mirror, the whole day is a total wash. I'll just keep thinking about it, turning it over in my head, wondering how I let myself slip, checking my reflection in the windows of the van when I'm packing up my gear... so yeah, it’s definitely an everyday thing. I just can't turn off that part of my brain, no matter how hard I try to focus on the work.
Do you feel anxious when you think about gaining weight?

Anxious... I mean, yeah. I guess anxious is probably the right word. Or at least, I get incredibly tense. It’s like this tight, heavy feeling right in the center of my chest that just kind of locks me up. 

Because, like I was saying before about those client dinners? Let’s say I actually cave and go to one, and I let my guard down. Or, I don't know, say I'm at a residential job and the homeowner is being super nice and brings out a tray of deli sandwiches for the crew, and I end up eating something with bread. Bread is just... it’s the worst for me, it just sits in my stomach like a brick. But anyway, if I do that, and then I wake up the next morning and go through my usual routine—you know, use the bathroom, strip down, step on the scale before I even look at my phone or start the coffee maker—if that number on the digital display is up even a little bit... like, even a fraction of a pound... my whole body just goes rigid. 

I get so tense I can feel it in my jaw. It’s just this immediate spike of panic, like, "Oh man, what did I do, I let it slip." And I can't just let it go. I can't just climb into the van, go to work, paint some ceilings, and forget about it. I have to fix it immediately. So the entire next day, I am just aggressively cutting back. If I normally have that one protein bar in the afternoon while I'm waiting for primer to dry, I’ll skip it. I’ll just drink extra black coffee, maybe chew some ice or just push through the empty feeling while I’m rolling out walls. 

I just have to make absolutely sure that whatever weight I put on from that bread or that dinner does not stick. It’s like... well, you know when you're painting trim and you get a tiny drip of latex on a nice hardwood floor? You don't just leave it there to dry and tell yourself you'll scrape it off later. You wipe it up immediately, right then and there, before it sets and ruins the finish. That’s exactly how I feel about the weight on the scale. I have to wipe it out before it becomes permanent. I have to get back to baseline. So, yeah, I definitely get anxious about it. It completely takes over my morning until I have a strict plan in my head to get that number back down.
Does your fear of gaining weight cause you significant distress?

Distress... well, yeah, I'd say so. I mean, it's not like I'm falling apart or anything. I have still been getting my painting jobs done, no problem there. Like I said, I'm up on the scaffolding, I'm taping, I'm cutting in, I'm delivering really good work to my clients. The business is totally fine. But... it’s everything else that gets complicated. The social stuff. 

I basically just avoid any kind of social plans now, especially those client meals I was talking about earlier, or even just grabbing a bite with the guys after wrapping up a big exterior job. I just dodge them completely. Because if I go... I know exactly how it’s going to play out. There's always going to be a big spread of heavy food, like pizza or burgers, and if I just sit there with a water or, you know, just pick at a side salad or whatever, people notice. And I just... I really do not want the situation to turn into people commenting on what I eat, or how I look. 

Because people always feel like they have the right to chime in, you know? They’ll be like, "Is that all you're eating after hauling buckets all day?" or "Come on man, have a beer, you're looking a little skinny anyway." And my heart just starts pounding the second they say that stuff. I absolutely hate having eyes on me like that, analyzing my plate, analyzing my body, trying to figure out why I'm not eating the same way they are. It’s exhausting, and it just makes me feel so on edge. 

So to avoid that whole nightmare, I just make up excuses. I'll tell them I need to go clean my spray rig, or I have to run to the hardware store before it closes to get more drop cloths for the next morning, or I'm just too beat from the sun. It’s just so much easier to go home and be by myself than to sit there and deal with their comments and their questions. So, yeah, I guess it does cause a lot of distress, because I'm basically isolating myself to protect my routine, but I just can't handle the anxiety of people watching me eat.
Are you finding it harder to keep up with your painting work because of your concerns about weight?

Harder? No, no, not at all. Honestly, that’s the part that really frustrates me about this whole situation. I mean... I know my friends, like the guys I occasionally sub out work to, and even my regular physician, they’ve all been acting super worried lately. They're always pulling me aside, giving me these concerned looks, asking if I'm feeling dizzy on the ladders or telling me I look too thin. My buddy Mike actually tried to take my extension ladder out of my hands the other day, acting like I couldn't carry it myself! I just... I really feel like everyone is completely overreacting. 

I mean, if you just look at the actual facts of the situation, right? Am I missing days? No. Am I messing up the trim or getting sloppy with my cut-ins? Absolutely not. I am still up at five in the morning every single day, loading the van, getting all the drop cloths and sprayers organized, and I'm usually at the site before anyone else even has their coffee. I'm still hauling five-gallon buckets of latex paint up two flights of stairs without asking for help. I'm still up on the scaffolding for eight, sometimes ten hours a day, keeping a wet edge on these massive vaulted ceilings. 

So when people start acting like I'm fragile, or like my weight is this massive crisis... I just don't get it. I really think they are making a mountain out of a molehill. Because if there was actually a serious problem, if I was really in some kind of danger like they seem to think, I wouldn't be able to do the physical labor, right? I'd be passing out or missing deadlines. But I'm not. I am showing up to every single job, I am getting my work done perfectly, and my clients are thrilled with the results. So no, it hasn't made the work harder at all. I just wish everyone would look at how much I'm getting done and realize they need to back off and stop worrying so much.
Are there any parts of your daily routine, outside of social situations, that you feel are being affected by your concerns about your weight?

Outside of the social stuff? Um... no, I really don't think so. I mean, I'm trying to think of what you would even mean by that, because my routine is just... it's just my routine, you know? It works perfectly fine for me. 

Like, if you look at a typical Tuesday or something, once I leave the job site, I just head straight home. I don't really do anything that would be affected by worrying about my weight or anything like that. I just pull the van into the driveway and start my evening prep, which honestly takes up most of my time anyway. You have to be incredibly meticulous in this line of work if you want to stay in business. Like, I’ll spend a solid hour or more just cleaning my spray rig. If you leave even a tiny bit of latex in the hose of a sprayer, the tip clogs up overnight, and then you're wasting an hour the next morning trying to pick it clean with a needle while the client is standing there wondering why you haven't started painting yet. So I run water through the lines, or mineral spirits if I was shooting oil-based primer on cabinets or something, and I just keep flushing it until it runs completely clear. 

And then I have to wash out my brushes. I only use these specific stiff nylon-polyester blend brushes for cutting in, and they cost like twenty bucks a pop, so you can't just let them get ruined. I'll stand at the utility sink in my basement with a wire brush just combing out the bristles for what feels like forever to make sure they keep their shape. And then after all that, you know, I check my emails, do some invoicing, maybe fold some canvas drop cloths so they're ready to just throw down the next morning without me having to untangle them on site. 

So, no, my evening is just normal business maintenance, maybe watching a little TV, and then going to sleep. I don't see how any of that is disrupted. I mean, sure, I have my specific food rules, like I told you, and I stick to my plan while I'm doing all those chores, but it doesn't stop me from getting the actual tasks done. Everything just runs on a very tight schedule. So yeah, I haven't really noticed any other parts of my day being messed up by this at all. I'm just living my life, taking care of my equipment, and getting ready for the next day. It's really just the people part, the social eating part, that gets complicated. Everything else is completely fine.
Are you ever unable to do something you want to do because you are worried about your weight?

Well, I mean... I guess I kind of already touched on this, but yeah. Like I said, I'm still getting my painting jobs done, no problem. The work itself is totally fine. I'm still up there on the ladders, getting everything taped and prepped and painted perfectly. But... it's the other stuff. The stuff I actually *want* to do sometimes, or at least used to want to do. 

Like, those client meals I mentioned earlier? Or grabbing a beer and some food with the guys after a massive exterior job? Sometimes I really do want to go. I mean, you spend ten hours a day with these guys, hauling buckets and breathing in fumes, you kind of build a bond, you know? And it would be nice to just sit back and shoot the breeze with them, or, you know, actually celebrate wrapping up a huge project with a client who's thrilled with the work. But I just... I can't. I avoid those plans completely now. 

And it's not because I don't want the company. It's just... I know exactly how it's going to go. If I go to the diner with the crew, or go to some fancy lunch with a client, there's going to be food everywhere. Heavy food. And I'm going to have to sit there, trying to figure out what I can possibly order, or just sitting there with a glass of water and a plain salad, and then... the comments start. I just absolutely do not want the situation to turn into people commenting on what I eat, or looking at me sideways, or making remarks about how I look. It just turns my stomach in knots even thinking about it. So, even if I really want to go hang out, even if I want to celebrate a job well done... I just make an excuse and go home. I just avoid it all because the worry about the food and the comments is just too much to handle.
Are there any activities or hobbies you've stopped doing or avoided because of your concerns about gaining weight?

Activities or hobbies? No, definitely not. I mean... honestly, between running the business, doing the actual labor, and keeping all my gear in top shape, I don't have a ton of free time for a million different hobbies anyway. But the stuff I do enjoy? I'm still doing it. 

Like, on the weekends, if I'm not catching up on quotes for new clients or doing exterior prep on a Saturday morning, I really like restoring old furniture. It kind of goes hand-in-hand with the painting, but it's more... quiet, you know? It's just me in the garage. I'll find these beat-up mid-century dressers at estate sales or flea markets, and I'll bring them back to my place. I spend hours just stripping off the old varnish. I use this citrus stripper now that doesn't smell as bad as the heavy chemical stuff, which is nice because I breathe in enough fumes during the week. And then I'm sanding it down through all the different grits—starting at like 80 grit to get the stubborn spots, and working my way all the way up to 220 or even 320 so the wood is smooth as glass. Then I'll rub in a Danish oil or maybe a custom stain I mixed up from leftover jobs. I was actually just out there this past Sunday working on this beautiful solid oak sideboard for like six hours straight. 

So, no, worrying about my weight hasn't stopped me from doing that at all. If anything, I'm probably doing it more these days because it keeps my hands busy and keeps me focused. 

And I still go fishing with my brother sometimes, too. We'll take his little aluminum johnboat out on the reservoir before the sun even comes up. I mean, yeah, I might not eat the donuts or the heavy sandwiches he brings on the boat anymore—I'll just bring my own specific things that I know are safe for me, or I'll just drink my black coffee from a thermos—but I'm still out there on the water, casting a line, you know? I haven't stopped living my life or doing the things I like to do. I haven't given up anything that actually matters to me. It really is just... exactly like I was saying before, it's just the social eating situations, the restaurants and the client lunches, that I avoid. Everything else, all my actual activities and projects, they're completely untouched by any of this.
Do you think your fear of gaining weight is affecting how you perceive your overall health?

Honestly, no, I don't think it's affecting my health at all. I mean, I know... I know some of my friends and my regular doctor are worried. They've made that pretty clear. Like, my buddy Mike who I sub out some drywall work to, he's been making comments lately, and my primary care doc brought it up at my last physical, acting like it's this huge crisis. But I really feel like they are just completely overreacting. I mean, they're acting like I'm falling apart, but look at what I actually do every day. 

If my health was actually in danger, how would I still be showing up to my jobs and getting all this physical work done? Just this past Tuesday, I was prepping a two-story foyer. Do you know what that entails? You're hauling a heavy-duty fiberglass A-frame ladder—the big 14-foot ones that weigh a ton—inside, maneuvering it around delicate hardwood floors without scratching anything, and then you're climbing up and down that thing all day with a gallon of ceiling flat in one hand and a roller pole in the other. You need serious core strength and stamina to do that for eight hours straight. And I'm doing it. I'm not passing out, I'm not calling in sick. I'm up there cutting in the crown molding with a completely steady hand. 

So when people start getting all concerned and telling me I need to worry about my health, I just kind of tune it out because the proof is in the pudding, you know? I'm running a successful business, I'm out there doing heavy manual labor, scraping, sanding, carrying five-gallon buckets of primer that weigh like sixty pounds each... I'm doing all of that without missing a beat. So I don't see how my health could possibly be failing if I'm still performing at that level. They just see things from the outside and make assumptions, but they don't see me actually getting the work done every single day. So yeah, they're definitely overreacting.
Are there any aspects of your daily routine, outside of eating and socializing, where you feel your concerns about weight are holding you back?

Well, honestly, I feel like we're kind of just going in circles here because it's exactly what I was talking about a few minutes ago. Outside of the eating and the socializing? No. Nothing else is holding me back at all. 

Like I said before, I have still been getting my painting jobs done, one hundred percent. I'm up at 5 AM every single day, loading the van, making sure I've got the right drop cloths, checking my inventory of rollers—you know, making sure I have the 3/8 inch nap for the smooth interior walls and the thicker ones for the exterior stucco—and I am on the job site by 7 AM sharp. I put in a full day's work, I do a meticulous job, and my clients are thrilled with the results. My daily routine as far as the business goes is totally fine.

The only place where any of this actually impacts my day-to-day life is just... well, those client meals and social plans I already mentioned. That's really it. And again, I just avoid them completely because I do not want the situation to turn into people commenting on what I eat or how I look. You know how people are, especially guys on a job site. They notice if you aren't eating a giant burger or if you just order a side salad, and then they have to make a whole big conversation out of it. It’s always, "Hey man, you sure you don't want some fries?" or "Is that all you're having after a ten-hour shift?" or they start making remarks about my weight. I just can't stand it. It makes me so incredibly uncomfortable to be under a microscope like that. 

So, yeah, to avoid all that hassle and the sideways glances, I just skip the client lunches and the after-work beers. But outside of avoiding those specific social situations? No, nothing else is holding me back. My routine is solid.
Are there any other activities or aspects of your daily life, outside of eating and socializing, where you feel like your concerns about weight are affecting your ability to participate or function?

I mean... Doc, I really feel like you're asking me the exact same question again. I don't know how many different ways I can explain this to you. No. There really isn't anything else. Like I literally just said a minute ago, my ability to function is completely fine. 

I have still been getting my painting jobs done, start to finish, without any issues. I was just working on this huge Victorian house exterior last week, doing all this intricate trim work, scraping century-old paint off these detailed wooden corbels up on the scaffolding. You can't do that kind of precision work if you aren't functioning, right? I'm getting the work done, and my clients are happy. 

The only thing—and I mean the absolute only thing—is the social stuff I keep bringing up. The client meals, the social plans after work, hanging out with the guys. I avoid them. I just skip them entirely now because I absolutely do not want the situation to turn into people commenting on what I eat or how I look. It never fails, you know? You sit down at a diner with a client to go over an estimate, or you go out with the crew, and if you don't order a massive plate of food, suddenly everyone's a nutritionist. They start asking why I'm not eating more, or staring at my plate, or making these little remarks about my body and what I'm putting in it. It's incredibly invasive and I just... I don't want to deal with it. It makes my skin crawl. So I avoid those specific meals and social plans. That is the only place this affects me. Everything else in my life, my work, my functioning... it's all exactly the same.
Do you think your weight concerns are affecting how you think about your overall health, beyond just your weight?

Doc, are you even listening to me? I feel like I'm talking to a brick wall here. We just went over this. I literally just told you about this. I don't know how to make it any clearer, but I'll try again. 

No. I don't think my weight concerns are affecting my overall health. At all. I know... look, I know my friends are worried. I know Mike is worried, and my regular doctor made a huge stink about it at my physical, acting like my heart's going to stop or something. They've all made their little comments and pulled me aside with their "serious" faces. But I really, truly feel like they are completely overreacting to the whole thing. 

I mean, how could my overall health be failing if I am still showing up to my jobs every single day and getting all this heavy, physical work done? I'm not sitting at a desk pushing pencils. I'm a painter. Do you know what it takes to prep and paint a whole house? Just yesterday, I was out there in the heat, power washing a massive wraparound porch, hauling hoses, moving heavy outdoor furniture, scrubbing away years of grime before I even touched a paintbrush. And then I'm carrying five-gallon buckets of exterior latex—those things are heavy, man—up and down ladders, reaching, stretching, bending over for hours on end. You can't do that if your health is compromised. You just can't. Your body would give out. 

But my body isn't giving out. I'm getting the work done. I'm finishing jobs on time, my clients are giving me five-star reviews, and I'm not missing a beat. target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about activities or hobbies stopped due to fear of gaining weight, which relates to functional impairment. The patient has already fully disclosed their functional impairment (avoiding client meals and social plans) in the previous turn and has no other symptoms or manifestations regarding other activities or hobbies.

patient.answer:
Activities or hobbies? No, definitely not. I mean... honestly, between running the business, doing the actual labor, and keeping all my gear in top shape, I don't have a ton of free time for a million different hobbies anyway. But the stuff I do enjoy? I'm still doing it. 

Like, on the weekends, if I'm not catching up on quotes for new clients or doing exterior prep on a Saturday morning, I really like restoring old furniture. It kind of goes hand-in-hand with the painting, but it's more... quiet, you know? It's just me in the garage. I'll find these beat-up mid-century dressers at estate sales or flea markets, and I'll bring them back to my place. I spend hours just stripping off the old varnish. I use this citrus stripper now that doesn't smell as bad as the heavy chemical stuff, which is nice because I breathe in enough fumes during the week. And then I'm sanding it down through all the different grits—starting at like 80 grit to get the stubborn spots, and working my way all the way up to 220 or even 320 so the wood is smooth as glass. Then I'll rub in a Danish oil or maybe a custom stain I mixed up from leftover jobs. I was actually just out there this past Sunday working on this beautiful solid oak sideboard for like six hours straight. 

So, no, worrying about my weight hasn't stopped me from doing that at all. If anything, I'm probably doing it more these days because it keeps my hands busy and keeps me focused. 

And I still go fishing with my brother sometimes, too. We'll take his little aluminum johnboat out on the reservoir before the sun even comes up. I mean, yeah, I might not eat the donuts or the heavy sandwiches he brings on the boat anymore—I'll just bring my own specific things that I know are safe for me, or I'll just drink my black coffee from a thermos—but I'm still out there on the water, casting a line, you know? I haven't stopped living my life or doing the things I like to do. I haven't given up anything that actually matters to me. It really is just... exactly like I was saying before, it's just the social eating situations, the restaurants and the client lunches, that I avoid. Everything else, all my actual activities and projects, they're completely untouched by any of this.

doctor.intent: determine if patient's fear of gaining weight is impacting their self-perception of health
doctor.question: Do you think your fear of gaining weight is affecting how you perceive your overall health?

target_item.name: Low_Weight_Severity_Non_Recognition
target_item.manifestation: I know my friends and the doctor are worried, but I feel like they are overreacting since I am still showing up to jobs and getting my work done.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's perception of their overall health, which directly addresses their lack of recognition of the seriousness of their current low body weight.

patient.answer:
Honestly, no, I don't think it's affecting my health at all. I mean, I know... I know some of my friends and my regular doctor are worried. They've made that pretty clear. Like, my buddy Mike who I sub out some drywall work to, he's been making comments lately, and my primary care doc brought it up at my last physical, acting like it's this huge crisis. But I really feel like they are just completely overreacting. I mean, they're acting like I'm falling apart, but look at what I actually do every day. 

If my health was actually in danger, how would I still be showing up to my jobs and getting all this physical work done? Just this past Tuesday, I was prepping a two-story foyer. Do you know what that entails? You're hauling a heavy-duty fiberglass A-frame ladder—the big 14-foot ones that weigh a ton—inside, maneuvering it around delicate hardwood floors without scratching anything, and then you're climbing up and down that thing all day with a gallon of ceiling flat in one hand and a roller pole in the other. You need serious core strength and stamina to do that for eight hours straight. And I'm doing it. I'm not passing out, I'm not calling in sick. I'm up there cutting in the crown molding with a completely steady hand. 

So when people start getting all concerned and telling me I need to worry about my health, I just kind of tune it out because the proof is in the pudding, you know? I'm running a successful business, I'm out there doing heavy manual labor, scraping, sanding, carrying five-gallon buckets of primer that weigh like sixty pounds each... I'm doing all of that without missing a beat. So I don't see how my health could possibly be failing if I'm still performing at that level. They just see things from the outside and make assumptions, but they don't see me actually getting the work done every single day. So yeah, they're definitely overreacting.

target_item.name: Functional Impairment

This directly addresses functional impairment, allowing the patient to reiterate that his work and other routines are unaffected, and only social/eating situations are impaired.

patient.answer:
Well, honestly, I feel like we're kind of just going in circles here because it's exactly what I was talking about a few minutes ago. Outside of the eating and the socializing? No. Nothing else is holding me back at all. 

Like I said before, I have still been getting my painting jobs done, one hundred percent. I'm up at 5 AM every single day, loading the van, making sure I've got the right drop cloths, checking my inventory of rollers—you know, making sure I have the 3/8 inch nap for the smooth interior walls and the thicker ones for the exterior stucco—and I am on the job site by 7 AM sharp. I put in a full day's work, I do a meticulous job, and my clients are thrilled with the results. My daily routine as far as the business goes is totally fine.

The only place where any of this actually impacts my day-to-day life is just... well, those client meals and social plans I already mentioned. That's really it. And again, I just avoid them completely because I do not want the situation to turn into people commenting on what I eat or how I look. You know how people are, especially guys on a job site. They notice if you aren't eating a giant burger or if you just order a side salad, and then they have to make a whole big conversation out of it. It’s always, "Hey man, you sure you don't want some fries?" or "Is that all you're having after a ten-hour shift?" or they start making remarks about my weight. I just can't stand it. It makes me so incredibly uncomfortable to be under a microscope like that. 

So, yeah, to avoid all that hassle and the sideways glances, I just skip the client lunches and the after-work beers. But outside of avoiding those specific social situations? No, nothing else is holding me back. My routine is solid.

doctor.intent: Determine if patient's fear of gaining weight is interfering with their daily life beyond social situations and eating habits
doctor.question: Are there any other activities or aspects of your daily life, outside of eating and socializing, where you feel like your concerns about weight are affecting your ability to participate or function?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking again about how concerns about weight are affecting my ability to participate or function in daily life, which directly maps to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
I mean... Doc, I really feel like you're asking me the exact same question again. I don't know how many different ways I can explain this to you. No. There really isn't anything else. Like I literally just said a minute ago, my ability to function is completely fine. 

I have still been getting my painting jobs done, start to finish, without any issues. I was just working on this huge Victorian house exterior last week, doing all this intricate trim work, scraping century-old paint off these detailed wooden corbels up on the scaffolding. You can't do that kind of precision work if you aren't functioning, right? I'm getting the work done, and my clients are happy. 

The only thing—and I mean the absolute only thing—is the social stuff I keep bringing up. The client meals, the social plans after work, hanging out with the guys. I avoid them. I just skip them entirely now because I absolutely do not want the situation to turn into people commenting on what I eat or how I look. It never fails, you know? You sit down at a diner with a client to go over an estimate, or you go out with the crew, and if you don't order a massive plate of food, suddenly everyone's a nutritionist. They start asking why I'm not eating more, or staring at my plate, or making these little remarks about my body and what I'm putting in it. It's incredibly invasive and I just... I don't want to deal with it. It makes my skin crawl. So I avoid those specific meals and social plans. That is the only place this affects me. Everything else in my life, my work, my functioning... it's all exactly the same.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's fear of gaining weight is impacting their self-perception of health beyond just weight
doctor.question: Do you think your weight concerns are affecting how you think about your overall health, beyond just your weight?

target_item.name: Low_Weight_Severity_Non_Recognition
target_item.manifestation: I know my friends and the doctor are worried, but I feel like they are overreacting since I am still showing up to jobs and getting my work done.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's perception of his overall health, which relates to whether he recognizes the seriousness of his low body weight and its impact on his health.

patient.answer:
Doc, are you even listening to me? I feel like I'm talking to a brick wall here. We just went over this. I literally just told you about this. I don't know how to make it any clearer, but I'll try again. 

No. I don't think my weight concerns are affecting my overall health. At all. I know... look, I know my friends are worried. I know Mike is worried, and my regular doctor made a huge stink about it at my physical, acting like my heart's going to stop or something. They've all made their little comments and pulled me aside with their "serious" faces. But I really, truly feel like they are completely overreacting to the whole thing. 

I mean, how could my overall health be failing if I am still showing up to my jobs every single day and getting all this heavy, physical work done? I'm not sitting at a desk pushing pencils. I'm a painter. Do you know what it takes to prep and paint a whole house? Just yesterday, I was out there in the heat, power washing a massive wraparound porch, hauling hoses, moving heavy outdoor furniture, scrubbing away years of grime before I even touched a paintbrush. And then I'm carrying five-gallon buckets of exterior latex—those things are heavy, man—up and down ladders, reaching, stretching, bending over for hours on end. You can't do that if your health is compromised. You just can't. Your body would give out. 

But my body isn't giving out. I'm getting the work done. I'm finishing jobs on time, my clients are giving me five-star reviews, and I'm not missing a beat. So when people start talking about my "overall health" like I'm some fragile piece of glass that's about to shatter, it's just ridiculous. They see me skipping a burger and suddenly they think I'm dying. It's just a massive overreaction, because the reality is, I'm out there working harder than most of the guys half my age. So no, my health is fine.
